# Ford Fusion 09 Starts Sometimes and Sometimes It Won't Start

Intermittent starting issues on a 2009 Ford Fusion are notoriously frustrating because they often disappear during diagnostics, leading to a cycle of false positives. Youâve already ruled out the most obvious culprits by replacing the starter and installing a new battery, yet the vehicle still exhibits this specific behavior: it cranks with a vacuum-like noise, electronics function when running, but the engine fails to start reliably. This pattern strongly suggests an issue with electrical continuity or a failing sensor rather than a dead battery or a seized motor.

The "vacuum noise" you hear when attempting to start is likely the starter solenoid engaging and drawing current through the ignition circuit. If the radio and lights work, your alternator is charging the system while the car is running, but the moment you cut the power to restart, the voltage drops momentarily. This indicates that the vehicle relies heavily on a stable resting charge in the battery and a pristine ground path.

One of the most common overlooked causes for this specific symptom set is corrosion or looseness at the chassis ground straps. Over time, vibration can cause the bolts securing the negative battery cable to the engine block or firewall to loosen. Similarly, oxidation on the contact points creates high resistance. When you turn the key, the starter draws a massive current spike (hundreds of amps). If the ground path has even a few ohms of extra resistance due to corrosion, that voltage drop can prevent the starter from turning fast enough to ignite the fuel mixture, resulting in no start. However, once the engine is running and the alternator is active, the system compensates for the poor ground, allowing the car to run fine until you shut it off again.

To diagnose this, locate the primary ground points on your Fusion 2009 model. Check the negative battery terminal clamp first; ensure it is tight and free of white or green oxidation. Then, trace the heavy black cable along the chassis. Look for grounding straps connecting the engine block to the unibody frame. These are often bolted near the firewall or underneath the intake manifold area. Remove the bolts, inspect the mating surfaces with a wire brush or sandpaper, and re-torque them securely. A visual inspection is rarely enough; you need to ensure physical contact is clean.

Another possibility lies in the ignition switch or the neutral safety switch (if applicable, though less common on automatic Fusions of this era). The ignition switch contains internal contacts that wear out over time. When these contacts become pitted or corroded, they may not pass voltage consistently between the "ON" and "START" positions. This would explain why the car works intermittently; sometimes the contact bridges just right, other times it doesn't. If you suspect this, you can try spraying a dielectric grease on the external ignition lock cylinder to rule out key alignment issues, though internal switch failure usually requires replacement.

Finally, consider the condition of the battery cables themselves. Even with a new battery, old cables can have internal breaks or severely corroded lugs at the other end (where they connect to the starter). The high current required by the starter cannot pass through corroded lugs effectively. Inspect both ends of the positive and negative cables for heat damage or discoloration, which indicates overheating due to poor connections.

If you are looking to sell this vehicle soon, resolving these electrical gremlins is critical. Buyers will inevitably notice a car that refuses to start 30% of the time and assume it is a catastrophic engine failure. By addressing ground integrity and verifying ignition switch function, you can eliminate the uncertainty and present a clean mechanical state. If the problem persists after tightening grounds and checking cables, the ignition switch itself is the next logical component to replace before listing the car.
